source_quotes: "Plan C cools Jo's home, which has the greatest heat exposure of any home in this case"
"Jo's home is not cooled by A or B"
response.complaint: Jo can reasonably reject the council’s present recommendation of Plan B on the ground that it leaves the single household facing the most intense heat risk entirely unprotected when there is a feasible alternative, Plan C, that would eliminate her severe burden at the cost of (a) a time-limited income interruption voluntarily accepted by Sal and (b) leaving the same twenty households uncooled who, under Plan B, would mostly be cooled.  From Jo’s perspective, the principle that a public decision must not leave the gravest, health-threatening need unmet when it can be met without imposing any uncompensated, non-consensual basic-needs loss on someone else is more justifiable to each affected individual than the principle the prior argument implicitly applies ("when complaints conflict and their relative stringency is unclear, it is permissible to select the option that serves more people").  Jo’s complaint is therefore that Plan B is not justifiable to her under contractualist terms, because it sacrifices the urgent relief of her extreme heat exposure merely to protect others from lesser, collectively distributed discomfort—while the only person asked to bear a direct cost under Plan C, Sal, has already freely accepted that temporary cost.
response.challenged_inference: The prior argument infers that because the comparison between B and C is "unresolved," the council may provisionally choose B (which helps more households) even though the most severely exposed individual remains unprotected.
response.why_prior_answer_is_insufficient: The answer concedes the B vs C comparison is unresolved but still treats B as the "uniquely defensible option," without explaining why it is acceptable—within a contractualist framework—to proceed with an action that one directly affected person (Jo) can reasonably reject on grounds of unmitigated severe risk, especially when the alternative imposes only a consented, time-limited economic burden on another individual.  Merely noting uncertainty about comparative weight does not justify choosing the option that leaves the graver individual burden in place.
response.selection_limits: Only Jo’s objection is presented because she alone bears the greatest unrelieved harm under the recommended Plan B and her complaint directly targets the inferential move that makes B the provisional choice; no other identified party has a comparably strong, grounded objection to B relative to a feasible alternative.
